replacement.title: Remain useful higher than the board battle
replacement.objective: Recognize high support while teammates contest the puck low.
replacement.briefing: F1 and Gold 1 contest a loose puck near the attacking-zone boards. F2 is nearer Gold’s net. YOU are assigned to support closer to the blue line than the battle until possession changes. Navy attacks the right net.
cues: YOU are assigned to support closer to the blue line than the battle until possession changes.

sources.section: PDF pages 7–8, team support and transition principles
sources.use: Supports the stated coaching principle. The setup, alternatives and suggested answers are original experimental coaching synthesis, not source-certified.

questions.prompt: What is the puck state at the board battle?

options.text: Loose and contested
Securely on F2’s stick
Already back at centre ice

questions.explanation: The puck marker is separate from F1 and Gold 1, as the briefing states.

questions.prompt: Which two jobs could high support serve?

options.text: Guaranteed possession merely by standing high
Help against a counterattack if Gold wins
An outlet if Navy wins control

questions.explanation: High support can preserve options in either outcome, but does not win the battle itself.

questions.prompt: Arrange a read from high support behind the battle.

options.text: Track who controls the puck
Check the high-slot space and opposing outlet
Adjust to the actual winner

questions.explanation: The high role is this exercise’s stated plan; a coach may assign a different forecheck elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a useful high-slot support example without joining the scrum.
questions.explanation: The reference keeps separation from the wall contest and access to middle ice. Other distances may suit the play.

questions.prompt: If F1 wins clean possession and looks inside, what could you offer?

options.text: An automatic move into F1’s crowded wall space
A visible high-slot option
A claim that the puck remains loose

questions.explanation: Control permits an attacking read, but you still need a reachable lane.

questions.prompt: Explain why the high forward’s position matters before the battle is decided.
questions.explanation: Describe both the possible outlet and defensive recovery roles, using the opponent’s location.

questions.prompt: Which Navy player is assigned the high support role?

options.text: YOU
F1
F2

questions.explanation: YOU are assigned the high support role. Reassess the outlet or defensive response when possession changes.

questions.prompt: Which two jobs can high support serve?

options.text: Be a reset if F1 wins it
Recover inside if Gold wins it
Join F1’s exact board lane

questions.explanation: Separation can help with either possession outcome. Joining the battle is a different choice that needs a coverage check.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare a middle support point closer to the blue line than the battle.
questions.explanation: The example remains separate from the board contest. Check Gold 2 and the actual puck winner before choosing the next route.

questions.prompt: What should change in your read when F1 wins clean possession?
questions.explanation: Check whether a useful passing lane has opened and what the coach’s support plan requires. A touch alone is not settled control, and winning possession does not automatically require leaving high support.

questions.prompt: Which named area lies between the two forward positions?

options.text: The defending crease at the Navy net
The centre faceoff circle
The high slot

questions.explanation: The forwards are on opposite sides of the high slot.

questions.prompt: Select two checks for an inside passing connection.

options.text: Whether F1 can see your target
Whether Gold 2 can reach the lane
Whether every cross-ice pass is automatically available

questions.explanation: Both the route and the carrier’s view matter; a large empty-looking space is not proof of safety.

questions.prompt: Arrange one way to create a clearer lane.

options.text: Locate the defenders near the route
Change your angle through useful space
Show the target and reassess

questions.explanation: The movement may create a pass or move a defender for another teammate.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward a high-slot pocket that changes the passing angle.
questions.explanation: This offers a shorter inside connection than the original far-side position. Gold 2’s response still needs checking.

questions.prompt: Gold 2 shifts into the high-slot connection. What might help now?

options.text: Use another support angle or leave room for D1
Assume the old connection remains clear
Treat Gold 2 as irrelevant because the pass is cross-ice

questions.explanation: The new defender position changes the read; the first support target is not permanent.

questions.prompt: Name the space you moved into and explain what made its passing angle different.
questions.explanation: Use “high slot” if describing the central pocket; connect the name to F1, Gold 2 and the route rather than only naming a zone.

questions.prompt: What should YOU call if Gold 2 enters the high-slot connection?

options.text: Gold 2 is in that lane; check another option
The lane is clear because Gold 2 moved
Ignore the slot

questions.explanation: Tell F1 that the intended route has changed. Do not call yourself open when Gold 2 occupies the connection.

questions.prompt: Which two cues decide whether a cross-ice look is usable?

options.text: Gold 1 and Gold 2’s positions
your visibility from F1
Assuming distance makes the pass safe

questions.explanation: Defender positions and a visible receiver determine the lane; distance alone does not make a pass safe.

questions.prompt: Move YOU into a high-slot pocket that changes F1’s passing angle.
questions.explanation: The pocket changes the line between F1 and YOU while Gold 1 and Gold 2 remain relevant; recheck whether any connection is usable.

questions.prompt: If Gold 2 shifts to cover the pocket from q9, what would YOU check before offering another spot?
questions.explanation: Check whether F1 can still see you and whether Gold 1 has also adjusted; re-spacing without checking both can trade one covered lane for another.

questions.prompt: Have YOU established possession in this freeze?

options.text: F2 already controls the pass
No, the pass is still loose
Yes, the puck is secured on the stick

questions.explanation: The briefing explicitly says the pass is unsettled, matching the loose marker.

questions.prompt: Which two cues affect the next action?

options.text: The quality of the arriving pass
A rule that every pass must be one-touched
How soon Gold 1 can pressure it

questions.explanation: Control and pressure determine what is practical; one-touch passing is not always available.

questions.prompt: Arrange one response to a difficult neutral-zone pass.

options.text: Read the bounce and approaching pressure
Establish control if there is time
Recheck the forward option

questions.explanation: Emergency touches may be needed under tighter pressure; this sequence assumes time to settle.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an example position for collecting the unsettled puck.
questions.explanation: The position moves toward the puck without pretending it is already controlled. Stick reach and bounce remain unmodelled.

questions.prompt: If the puck arrives flat and F2’s lane is clearly available, what might change?

options.text: You must always take several extra touches
Gold 1 no longer needs to be checked
An earlier pass may be practical

questions.explanation: A better reception can create an earlier option, but only while the lane remains available.

questions.prompt: If Gold 1 could already reach the puck, how might your response change?
questions.explanation: There may be less time to settle it. Compare a controlled touch, protection or an available outlet using the actual pressure and puck path.

questions.prompt: What should YOU call while F2’s lane is available but the puck is unsettled?

options.text: Not settled; give me a short option
One-touch now no matter the pressure
F2 cannot be used

questions.explanation: Communicate that the puck is unsettled and ask for support. Whether to settle, protect or redirect still depends on pressure.

questions.prompt: Which two cues affect the next touch?

options.text: F2’s higher position
Gold 1’s approach
The pass being difficult no longer matters

questions.explanation: F2’s lane and Gold 1’s pressure shape whether to settle, protect or move it; a difficult reception remains relevant.

questions.prompt: Move YOU closer to the unsettled puck to compare a collecting angle.
questions.explanation: The example is nearer the puck. Gold 1 is also approaching, so check time and reach before treating the puck as controlled.

questions.prompt: What would you need to see before recommending a one-touch pass?
questions.explanation: Check the arriving puck’s speed and path, F2’s readiness and the passing lane. A one-touch redirects the arriving puck without first settling it; if that touch is not practical, compare other available actions.

questions.prompt: What result is still unknown?

options.text: Who will control the next touch
Which net Navy attacks
Whether YOU are a Navy player

questions.explanation: The puck is loose between opponents and no winner is stated.

questions.prompt: Pick two outcomes to prepare for.

options.text: A guaranteed attack because F1 is close
A defensive response if Gold 1 wins
A support option if F1 wins

questions.explanation: A contested puck calls for more than one conditional plan.

questions.prompt: Arrange a read before committing ahead of this contest.

options.text: Observe the contested touch
Identify the actual puck owner
Commit to the useful support job

questions.explanation: Anticipation can help, but the question does not grant control based on proximity.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to support the contest while retaining access to middle ice.
questions.explanation: The reference is behind the battle and more central. It can support either outcome but is not a universal distance.

questions.prompt: Gold 1 now takes clear control. What changes?

options.text: Nothing until Gold 1 reaches the net
The recovery and defensive-support read
An automatic pass from F1 is still assured

questions.explanation: Recognized possession changes the support job before the attack is fully developed.

questions.prompt: How is anticipation different from assuming the puck has already been won?
questions.explanation: Anticipation keeps conditional alternatives; an assumption treats uncertain possession as settled.

questions.prompt: What should YOU call while F1 and Gold 1 contest the loose puck?

options.text: Both outcomes are live; I am middle support
F1 has won it
Gold 1 has won it

questions.explanation: Name your support position without claiming a winner. Reassess an outlet or defensive job once control is clear.

questions.prompt: Which two outcomes should YOU prepare for?

options.text: F1 controls and needs an outlet
Gold 1 controls and attacks
Assuming F1 has already won

questions.explanation: Preparing both outcomes avoids a false possession assumption; if the touch becomes clear, commit to that new job.

questions.prompt: Move YOU into a support position behind F1 that still protects the middle.
questions.explanation: The middle-support spot helps F1 if Navy wins while preserving a recovery lane if Gold wins; if possession settles, move with the new carrier.

questions.prompt: What does keeping both outcomes available protect YOU from doing?
questions.explanation: Anticipation keeps both retrieval and defensive lanes available until ownership is clear; assuming possession can leave the middle uncovered.

Evaluate a faceoff rule violation
Pursue the loose puck near the side boards

questions.prompt: Which two facts should update that plan?

options.text: Whether C’s inside support remains available
Who gains control first
The assumption that all faceoffs use this arrangement

questions.explanation: A planned role still responds to possession and support.

questions.prompt: Arrange one follow-up to this draw.

options.text: Locate the loose puck
Check the opponent and assigned support
Pursue or adjust to the actual control

questions.explanation: The sequence is a suggested response under the stated drill plan, not a universal faceoff play.

questions.prompt: If Gold 1 controls the puck before you arrive, what should you do?

options.text: Reassess pressure and C’s support
Act as if the draw was already won by Navy
Follow the retrieval route with no new read

questions.explanation: The opponent’s control changes the action even when the pre-draw plan was clear.

questions.prompt: Why does knowing a faceoff plan not remove the need to read the puck?
questions.explanation: A plan assigns starting responsibilities; the bounce, opponent and possession decide what is possible next.

questions.prompt: Which Navy teammate is assigned to stay inside?

options.text: D1
C
Gold 1

questions.explanation: C has the stated inside assignment. If Gold wins control, reassess pressure and coverage together.

questions.prompt: Which two facts should update that faceoff plan?

options.text: The puck remains loose
Gold 1’s route to the puck
The assumption that Navy already controls the puck

questions.explanation: The puck’s actual state and Gold 1’s approach shape the next action.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward the side-board puck while leaving space for C inside.
questions.explanation: The example approaches the loose puck and stays separate from C. Reassess if Gold gains control.

questions.prompt: Why should C stay inside instead of also chasing the loose puck toward the boards?
questions.explanation: If both YOU and C converge on the puck near the boards, the middle of the ice opens up; C staying inside keeps that space covered in case Gold 1 wins the puck and looks to counter.
